source_text: Quid est ergo, Non ex sanguine nec ex voluntate carnis nec ex voluntate viri, sed ex deo natus est? Hoc quidem capitulo ego potius utar cum aduleratores eius obduxero. Sic enim scriptum esse contendunt: Nem ex sanguine nec ex carnis voluntate nec ex viri, sed ex deo nati sunt, quasi supra dictos credentes in nomine eius designet, ut ostendat esse semen illud arcanum electorum et spiritalium, quod sibi imbuunt. Quomodo autem ita erit, cum omnes, qui credunt in nomine domini, pro communi lege generis humani ex sanguine et ex carnis et ex viri voluntate nascantur, etiam Valentinus ipse? Adeo singulariter, ut de domino, scriptum est: Et ex deo natus est. Merito, quia verbum dei, et cum verbo dei spiritus, et in spiritu dei virtus, et quicquid dei est Christus. Qua caro autem, non ex sanguine nec ex carnis et viri voluntate, quia ex dei voluntate verbum caro factum est. Ad carnem enim, non ad verbum, pertinet negatio formalis nostrae nativitatis, quia caro sic habebat nasci, non verbum. Negans autem ex carnis quoque voluntate natum cur non negavit etiam ex substantia carnis? Neque enim quia ex sanguine negavit, substantiam carnis renuit, sed materiam seminis, quam constat sanguinis esse calorem, ut despumatione mutatum in coagulum sanguinis feminae. Nam ex coagulo in caseo vis est substantiae quam medicando constringit, id est lactis. Intellegimus ergo ex concubitu nativitatem domini negatam, quod sapit voluntas viri et carnis, non ex vulvae participatione. Et quid utique tam exaggeranter inculcavit non ex sanguine nec ex carnis voluntate aut viri natum nisi quia ea erat caro quam ex concubitu natam nemo dubitaret? Negans porro ex concubitu non negavit ex carne, immo confirmavit ex carne, quia non proinde negavit ex carne sicut ex concubitu negavit. Oro vos, si dei spiritus non de vulva carnem participaturus descendit in vulvam, cur descendit in vulvam? Potuit enim extra eam fieri caro spiritalis; simplicius multo quam intra vulvam fieret extra vulvam. Sine causa ea se intulit unde nihil extulit. Sed non sine causa descendit in vulvam. Ergo ex illa accepit, quia si non ex illa accepit, sine causa in illam descendit, maxime eius qualitatis caro futurus quae non erat vulvae, id est spiritalis.
thought_title: The Flesh Born of God, Not of Human Will
orientation: Tertullian is refuting the Valentinian reading of John 1:13, arguing that the verse's singular 'born of God' refers to Christ alone, and that denying his birth from blood and human will does not deny his birth from Mary's flesh.
pass_a_gloss: What then is, 'Not from blood nor from the will of the flesh nor from the will of a man, but from God he was born'? This chapter I shall rather use when I have brought in its adulterators. For they contend that it was written thus: 'Not from blood nor from the will of the flesh nor from a man, but from God they were born,' as if it designated the above-mentioned believers in his name, so that it may show that there is that secret seed of the elect and spiritual ones, which they imbue themselves with. But how will it be so, when all who believe in the name of the Lord, by the common law of the human race, are born from blood and from the will of the flesh and of a man, even Valentinus himself? So singularly, as about the Lord, it is written: 'And from God he was born.' Rightly, because he is the Word of God, and with the Word of God the Spirit, and in the Spirit of God the power, and whatever is of God, Christ is. But as for the flesh, not from blood nor from the will of the flesh and of a man, because from the will of God the Word was made flesh. For to the flesh, not to the Word, belongs the denial of the form of our birth, because the flesh had to be born thus, not the Word. But denying that he was born also from the will of the flesh, why did he not deny also from the substance of the flesh? For not because he denied from blood did he reject the substance of the flesh, but the material of the seed, which it is agreed is the heat of blood, as by foaming it is changed into the coagulation of the blood of the female. For from the coagulation in cheese there is the force of the substance which by curdling it solidifies, that is, of milk. We understand therefore that the birth of the Lord is denied from intercourse, which the will of a man and of the flesh savors of, not from the participation of the womb. And why indeed did he so emphatically inculcate that he was not born from blood nor from the will of the flesh or of a man, except because that was flesh which no one would doubt was born from intercourse? Denying further from intercourse he did not deny from flesh, rather he confirmed from flesh, because he did not deny from flesh in the same way as he denied from intercourse. I ask you, if the Spirit of God, not about to share flesh from the womb, descended into the womb, why did he descend into the womb? For spiritual flesh could have been made outside it; much more simply than within the womb would it be made outside the womb. Without cause he brought himself into that from which he brought out nothing. But not without cause did he descend into the womb. Therefore he received from it, because if he did not receive from it, without cause he descended into it, especially since he was going to be flesh of that quality which was not of the womb, that is, spiritual.

choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of corrupting a text, matching Tertullian's polemical tone against those who alter Scripture.

choices.english: by foaming it is changed into the coagulation of the blood of the female
choices.why: Renders the physiological process literally, keeping the medical-scientific register Tertullian uses to explain seed as heated blood.
rejected: by frothing it turns into the clotting of the woman's blood

choices.why: Concubitus means sexual union; 'intercourse' is the plain English equivalent and fits the context of denying birth from human will.
Keeps the rhetorical force of the adverb and verb, showing Tertullian's point that John stressed the denial.
The future participle conveys purpose or intention; 'about to share' preserves the sense that the Spirit did not intend to take flesh from the womb.

pass_b_english: What then does it mean, “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but born of God” (John 1:13)? I will rather make use of this passage myself, once I have refuted those who adulterate it. They contend that it was written this way: “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of man, but they were born of God,” as if it designated the believers in his name mentioned above, to show that there is that secret seed of the elect and spiritual ones, which they steep themselves in. But how will that be, when all who believe in the name of the Lord are born of blood and of the will of the flesh and of man, by the common law of the human race—even Valentinus himself? It is written in the singular, as of the Lord: “And he was born of God.” Rightly so, because he is the Word, and with the Word the Spirit, and in the Spirit of God the power, and whatever is of God, Christ is. But as for his flesh, it was not of blood nor of the will of the flesh and of man, because by the will of God the Word became flesh (John 1:14). The denial of our formal birth pertains to the flesh, not to the Word, because the flesh had to be born this way, not the Word.

But when he denied that he was born of the will of the flesh, why did he not also deny that he was of the substance of flesh? For in denying that he was of blood, he did not reject the substance of flesh, but the material of seed, which is known to be the heat of blood, changed by foaming into the coagulation of the blood of the female. For in cheese the curd holds the force of a substance, that is, of milk, which the curdling binds together. We understand therefore that the Lord's birth from intercourse is denied, which the will of man and of the flesh savors of, not from participation in the womb. And why did he so emphatically inculcate that he was not born of blood nor of the will of the flesh or of man, except because it was flesh which no one would doubt was born from intercourse? In denying then that he was from intercourse, he did not deny that he was from flesh; rather, he confirmed that he was from flesh, because he did not deny he was from flesh in the same way as he denied he was from intercourse.

I ask you, if the Spirit of God descended into the womb not about to share flesh from the womb, why did he descend into the womb? For spiritual flesh could have been made outside it; much more simply would it have been made outside the womb than inside the womb. Without cause he brought himself into that from which he took nothing out. But he did not descend into the womb without cause. Therefore he received from it, because if he did not receive from it, he descended into it without cause—especially since he was about to be flesh of a quality which did not belong to the womb, that is, spiritual.

problems.why: Tertullian uses 'flesh' (caro) and 'body' (corpus) technically distinct but often interchangeably; reader cannot track when distinction matters.
problems.fix: Note when 'body' means soma/corpus vs. when 'flesh' means sarx/caro.

problems.quote: why did he not also deny that he was of the substance of flesh? For because he denied he was of blood, he did not reject the substance of flesh, but the material of seed
problems.why: Logical connector 'For because' is awkward; argument about 'substance' vs. 'material' is technical and compressed.
problems.fix: Simplify: 'He denied blood (i.e., male seed), not flesh itself.'

problems.quote: not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but born of God
problems.why: John 1:13; but Tertullian argues this refers to Christ, not believers. Textual variant: some manuscripts have 'who was born' (singular) vs. 'who were born' (plural).
problems.fix: Note textual variant and Tertullian's reading.

problems.why: The sentence is nearly incomprehensible; the analogy between blood coagulation and cheese-making is lost in awkward syntax.
problems.fix: Rewrite for clarity: 'Just as milk curdles into cheese, blood coagulates into the substance of flesh.'

fixed: The glossary problem is not a translation error; the English uses 'flesh' for caro throughout, and 'body' does not appear in this section, so no edit is needed.
The logical connector 'For because' is awkward; changed to 'For in denying' to clarify the argument while staying close to the source 'Neque enim quia ex sanguine negavit'.
The Scripture citation is correct as rendered; the textual variant is a scholarly note, not a translation error, and the English already reflects Tertullian's singular reading.
The cheese analogy sentence was awkward; simplified to 'which curdling binds' to match the source 'quam medicando constringit' more clearly.

fixed: The sentence about coagulation in cheese was unclear and read like a word-for-word gloss. The source says 'Nam ex coagulo in caseo vis est substantiae quam medicando constringit, id est lactis' — 'For from the curd in cheese there is the power of the substance which by curdling it solidifies, that is, of milk.' The English now clarifies that the curd in cheese has the substance-making power that curdling solidifies, referring to milk.

problems.fix: For in cheese the curd holds the force of a substance, that is, of milk, which the curdling binds together.

problems.quote: So it was written uniquely, as about the Lord
problems.source_quote: Adeo singulariter, ut de domino, scriptum est
problems.why: singulariter means the verb is singular (natus est), against the heretics' plural, not that the wording is unique.
problems.fix: It is written in the singular, as of the Lord: “And he was born of God.”
problems.ruling: "Adeo singulariter" answers the heretics' plural "nati sunt" with singular "natus est"; "uniquely" hides this grammatical-number argument and misleads the reader.

last_rejected.quote: especially since he was about to be flesh of a quality which did not belong to the womb, that is, spiritual.
last_rejected.source_quote: maxime eius qualitatis caro futurus quae non erat vulvae, id est spiritalis.
last_rejected.why: Presents spiritual flesh as what he was going to be. It belongs to the vain-descent counterfactual, the view just rejected.
last_rejected.fix: he descended into it without cause—above all if he was to be flesh of a quality the womb has not, that is, spiritual.
last_rejected.ruling: The English follows the source's 'maxime eius qualitatis caro futurus quae non erat vulvae, id est spiritalis' and keeps the reductio's 'if he did not receive from it' frame. No translation error.
